div.head: Section 530
div.p: SOCRATES. Welcome, Ion. Where have you come from now? Are you coming from your home in Ephesus?
ION. No, Socrates, I have come from Epidaurus, from the festival of Asclepius.
SOCRATES. Do the Epidaurians hold a contest for rhapsodes in honor of the god?
ION. They certainly do, and for every other kind of musical art as well.
SOCRATES. And did you compete? How did it go?
ION. We carried off the first prize, Socrates!
SOCRATES. Excellent! See to it that we win at the Panathenaea too.
ION. That will happen, god willing.

SOCRATES. You know, Ion, I have often envied you rhapsodes for your profession. It requires you to always be dressed in beautiful garments and look your best. But more than that, it requires you to constantly engage with the many fine poets, especially Homer, the best and most divine of them all. And not only to memorize his verses, but to understand his true meaning—that is truly enviable! For no one can be a good rhapsode if he does not understand what the poet is saying. The rhapsode must serve as an interpreter of the poet's thought to his listeners, and to do this well requires understanding.

ION. You speak the truth, Socrates. In fact, that part of my profession has taken the most effort. I believe that I speak about Homer better than anyone else alive. Neither Metrodorus of Lampsacus, nor Stesimbrotus of Thasos, nor Glaucon, nor anyone else who has ever lived, has had so many and such fine thoughts to offer about Homer as I do.
SOCRATES. That is good to hear, Ion. For clearly you will not grudge giving me a display of your skill.
ION. Indeed, Socrates, it is well worth hearing how beautifully I have adorned Homer. I believe the Homeridae ought to award me a golden crown for my work.
SOCRATES. I certainly intend to find time to hear you. But for now, just answer me this: are you skilled only in Homer, or in Hesiod and Archilochus as well?
ION. No, no. Only in Homer. I find that to be quite sufficient.

div.head: Section 531
div.p: SOCRATES. Is there any subject on which Homer and Hesiod agree?
ION. Yes, I believe there are many.
SOCRATES. In those matters where they agree, would you be able to explain what Homer says better than what Hesiod says?
ION. I would explain them equally well, Socrates, in the matters where they agree.
SOCRATES. But what about the matters on which they disagree? For instance, both Homer and Hesiod speak about divination.
ION. Yes.
SOCRATES. Now, if the two poets disagree about divination, who would explain those differences better: you, or an expert diviner?
ION. A diviner.
SOCRATES. And if you were the diviner, and could explain their agreements, wouldn't you also be able to explain their disagreements?
ION. Clearly.

SOCRATES. Then why are you skilled only in Homer, and not in Hesiod and the other poets? Does Homer speak about anything different from what all the other poets speak about? Does he not mainly speak about war, about human association—good and bad, laymen and craftsmen—about the gods associating with each other and with men, about the heavens and the underworld, and the origins of gods and heroes? Are these not the very subjects of Homer's poetry?
ION. They are, Socrates.
SOCRATES. And do not the other poets write about these exact same subjects?
ION. Yes, Socrates, but they have not written about them in the same way Homer has.
SOCRATES. How do you mean? Do they do it worse?
ION. Much worse.
SOCRATES. And Homer does it better?
ION. Better by far! By Zeus, he is the best.

SOCRATES. Well now, my dear Ion, when people are discussing numbers, and one person speaks better than the rest, is it not the same person who can judge both the one speaking well and those speaking badly? Namely, the one who possesses the art of arithmetic?
ION. Yes.

SOCRATES. And when many people are discussing what sorts of foods are healthy, and one person speaks best, is it the person who recognizes the best speaker who also recognizes that the others are speaking worse? Or is it a different person? Is it not the doctor who judges both?
ION. Yes, the doctor.

div.head: Section 532
div.p: SOCRATES. Is it not generally true in all arts that the same person who is a competent judge of the one who speaks well is also a competent judge of the one who speaks poorly? For if a person cannot recognize the one who speaks poorly, he will surely not recognize the one who speaks well about the same subject.
ION. That is true.
SOCRATES. Therefore, the same man is skilled in both?
ION. Yes.
SOCRATES. And you say that Homer and the other poets, including Hesiod and Archilochus, speak about the same things, but not equally well. Homer speaks well, while the others speak worse.
ION. And I speak the truth.
SOCRATES. But if you recognize that Homer speaks well, you must also recognize that the others speak worse than he does.
ION. It seems so.

SOCRATES. Excellent! Then if we say that Ion is skilled concerning Homer, we must also say he is skilled concerning the other poets. For you agreed that the same person is a competent judge of all who speak on the same subjects.

ION. Then how do you explain this, Socrates: when anyone discusses any other poet, I pay no attention. I have nothing to contribute and I simply fall asleep. But as soon as anyone mentions Homer, I immediately wake up, pay close attention, and have plenty to say.

SOCRATES. That is not difficult to guess, my friend. It is obvious to everyone that you do not speak about Homer by art or by knowledge. If you were speaking by an art, you would be able to speak about all the other poets as well. Let me explain. Is there not an entire art of poetry?
ION. Yes, there is.
SOCRATES. And when someone considers any other entire art, isn't the method of inquiry the same? Let me give you an example, Ion.
ION. By Zeus, Socrates, please do! I love hearing you wise men speak.

SOCRATES. I wish we were wise, Ion. But you rhapsodes and actors, and the poets whose songs you sing, are the wise ones. I only speak the truth as a common man. Let us look at what I just said. Does it not hold true for painting, that there is a whole art of painting?
ION. Yes.

div.head: Section 533
div.p: SOCRATES. And there are, and have been, many painters, good and bad?
ION. Certainly.

SOCRATES. Have you ever known someone who is skilled at showing what Polygnotus paints well and what he paints poorly, but who is completely unable to judge any other painter? Someone who falls asleep when other painters are discussed, but wakes up and has plenty to say only when Polygnotus is mentioned?
ION. No, by Zeus, I have not.
SOCRATES. And in sculpture? Have you ever known someone who could judge the skill of Daedalus or Epeius, but who had nothing to say about the work of other sculptors?
ION. No, I have never seen anyone like that either.

SOCRATES. And I imagine the same holds true for flute-playing, lyre-playing, or singing to the cithara. You have never known someone who was clever at judging the flute-playing of Olympus, but who fell asleep and had nothing to say when judging another flute-player.

ION. I cannot argue with you on that point, Socrates. But I know this much about myself: I speak about Homer better and more abundantly than anyone else, and everyone else says I speak well about him. But I do not speak well about the others. Tell me why this is so.

SOCRATES. I will tell you, Ion, what I think this is. As I said before, this ability you have to speak well about Homer is not an art in you. It is a divine power that moves you, just like the power in the stone that Euripides called a magnet, though most call it the Heraclean stone. This stone not only attracts iron rings, but also imparts its power to the rings themselves, so they can attract other rings. Sometimes a long chain of iron rings is formed, all depending on the power of the original stone. In the same way, the Muse first inspires people herself, and then through these inspired people a chain of others is suspended, all sharing in the inspiration. For all good epic poets do not compose their beautiful poems by art, but because they are inspired and possessed.

div.head: Section 534
div.p: SOCRATES. And it is the same with the good lyric poets. Just as those who engage in Corybantic frenzies are not in their right minds when they dance, so too the lyric poets are not in their right minds when they compose their beautiful songs. Once they embark on harmony and rhythm, they become frenzied and possessed, like Bacchic maidens who draw milk and honey from the rivers only when they are possessed, but not when they are in their right minds. The souls of the lyric poets do the same, as they themselves admit. For they tell us that they gather their melodies from honeyed springs in the gardens and glens of the Muses, flying like bees, and bringing them to us. And they speak the truth. A poet is a light and winged and sacred thing. He is unable to compose poetry until he is inspired and out of his mind, and his reason is no longer within him. As long as he retains his reason, no human is capable of composing poetry or prophesying. Therefore, since they compose not by art but by divine dispensation, each poet is only able to compose beautifully what the Muse has urged him to do. One is good at making dithyrambs, another praises, another dance songs, another epics, and another iambics; but in other types, each is worthless. Because they speak these things not by art, but by divine power. If they knew how to speak well on one subject by art, they would know how to speak well on all subjects. This is why the god takes away their minds and uses them as his servants, just as he uses prophets and divine seers, so that we who hear them may know that it is not these men who are saying these wonderful things—since they have no mind—but that it is the god himself speaking to us through them. The greatest proof of this is Tynnichus the Chalcidian, who never composed a single poem worth mentioning, except for the one paean that everyone sings, perhaps the most beautiful of all lyrical poems. As he himself said, it was simply an "invention of the Muses." In this, it seems, the god showed us clearly, so we wouldn't doubt it, that these beautiful poems are not human or the work of humans, but divine and the work of gods; and that the poets are nothing but interpreters of the gods, each possessed by the god who possesses him. Do I not speak the truth, Ion?

div.head: Section 535
div.p: ION. By Zeus, you certainly do! You somehow touch my soul with your words, Socrates, and it seems to me that it is indeed by divine dispensation that good poets interpret these things from the gods to us.
SOCRATES. And do not you rhapsodes, in turn, interpret the words of the poets?
ION. We do.
SOCRATES. So you are interpreters of interpreters?
ION. Exactly.

SOCRATES. Now tell me this, Ion, and do not hide anything from me. When you speak epic verses well and strike the spectators with the greatest awe—when you sing of Odysseus leaping upon the threshold, revealing himself to the suitors and pouring out the arrows at his feet, or of Achilles rushing at Hector, or of the pitiful things concerning Andromache, Hecuba, or Priam—are you in your right mind at that moment, or are you beside yourself? Does your soul, through inspiration, believe it is present at the very events you are describing, whether in Ithaca or Troy?

ION. What a clear proof you bring me, Socrates! I will tell you without hiding anything. When I recount a tale of pity, my eyes fill with tears. When I tell of something terrifying or dreadful, the hair on my head stands up from fear, and my heart pounds.

SOCRATES. Now tell me, Ion, is a man in his right mind when, dressed in colorful robes and golden crowns, he starts weeping at a sacrifice or festival, though he has lost none of his finery? Or when he shrinks back in fear, standing among twenty thousand friendly people, none of whom is stripping or wronging him?
ION. No, by Zeus, Socrates, he is not entirely in his right mind, if I am to speak the truth.
SOCRATES. And are you aware that you produce these same effects on most of the spectators?

ION. I know it very well. For I look down from the platform and see them weeping, or gazing at me in terror and awe, matching my words. I must pay close attention to them, for if I make them weep, I will laugh when I collect my money; but if I make them laugh, I will weep for losing my pay.

div.head: Section 536
div.p: SOCRATES. Do you realize, then, that the spectator is the last of those iron rings I mentioned, which receive their power from the Heraclean stone? You, the rhapsode or actor, are the middle ring, and the poet himself is the first one. Through all of you, the god draws the souls of men wherever he wishes, transmitting the power from one to another. Just as from the magnet, a huge chain of chorus members, masters, and assistant masters is suspended sideways from the rings that hang from the Muse. One poet is suspended from one Muse, another from another—we call this being "possessed," for he is held fast by her. And from these first rings—the poets—other rings are suspended and inspired, some attached to Orpheus, some to Musaeus; but the majority are possessed and held fast by Homer. You are one of these, Ion. You are possessed by Homer. When someone sings the verses of another poet, you fall asleep and are at a loss for words; but when someone strikes a chord of your poet, you instantly awaken, your soul dances, and you have plenty to say. For you do not say what you say about Homer by an art or by knowledge, but by divine dispensation and possession. Just as the Corybantes eagerly respond only to the melody of the god by whom they are possessed, and have plenty of gestures and words for that tune but ignore all others, so you, Ion, are full of words when someone mentions Homer, but are at a loss regarding the others. The reason you can speak beautifully about Homer but not the others is exactly what you ask: it is not by an art, but by divine dispensation.

ION. You speak well, Socrates. But I would be surprised if you could speak well enough to persuade me that I praise Homer because I am possessed and mad. I do not think I would seem that way to you, if you heard me speaking about him.
SOCRATES. But I do wish to hear you! However, not before you answer this for me: on which of the subjects Homer speaks about do you speak well? Surely you do not speak well on all of them.
ION. Rest assured, Socrates, there is nothing he speaks of that I do not speak well on.
SOCRATES. Surely not the things you happen not to know, even if Homer speaks of them?
ION. And what is there that Homer speaks of that I do not know?

div.head: Section 537
div.p: SOCRATES. Does not Homer speak in many places, and quite fully, about arts? For instance, chariot driving. If I can remember the verses, I will recite them to you.
ION. I will recite them! I remember them.
SOCRATES. Tell me, then, what Nestor says to his son Antilochus, advising him to be careful at the turning post in the horse race in honor of Patroclus.

ION. "Lean yourself in the well-built chariot A little to the left of the horses; but call to the right-hand horse And goad him on, giving him slack in the reins. Let your left-hand horse closely skim the turning post, So that the hub of the well-made wheel seems To touch the edge; but avoid striking the stone."
SOCRATES. That is enough. Now, Ion, who would know better whether Homer speaks correctly here or not: a doctor or a charioteer?
ION. A charioteer, certainly.
SOCRATES. Because he possesses that specific art, or for some other reason?
ION. Because he possesses the art.

SOCRATES. Has not a specific capability been granted to each of the arts by the god to know a particular work? For we do not know the things known by the art of piloting through the art of medicine, do we?
ION. Of course not.
SOCRATES. Nor the things known by medicine through the art of building?
ION. No.
SOCRATES. And is this not true for all arts? What we know by one art we do not know by another? But first answer me this: do you agree that there is one art, and another that is different?
ION. Yes.
SOCRATES. I judge that when one kind of knowledge is about one thing, and another kind of knowledge is about another thing, they are two different arts. Is that how you judge it too?
ION. Yes.

div.head: Section 538
div.p: SOCRATES. For if it were the same knowledge of the same things, why would we call it one art here and another art there, when we could know the same things from either? For example, I know there are five fingers here, and you know the same thing about them. If I asked you whether we both know this by the same art—arithmetic—or by different ones, you would say the same art.
ION. Yes.

SOCRATES. Now answer what I was asking earlier. Does it seem to you that this applies to all arts: the same art necessitates knowing the same things, and a different art necessitates knowing different things? If it is a different art, it must necessarily know different things.
ION. Yes, Socrates, that is how it seems to me.
SOCRATES. Therefore, whoever does not possess a certain art will not be able to correctly recognize what is spoken or done well within that art.
ION. True.
SOCRATES. So in the verses you just recited about chariot driving, who will judge better whether Homer speaks well: you or a charioteer?
ION. A charioteer.
SOCRATES. Because you are a rhapsode, not a charioteer.
ION. Yes.
SOCRATES. And the art of a rhapsode is different from the art of a charioteer.
ION. Yes.
SOCRATES. If it is a different art, it possesses knowledge of different things.
ION. Yes.

SOCRATES. Consider what Homer says about medicine, when Hecamede gives a potion to wounded Machaon. He says something like: "Upon Pramnian wine she grated goat's cheese With a brazen grater, and an onion as a relish for the drink." Is it the doctor's art or the rhapsode's art that can judge correctly whether Homer speaks well here?
ION. The doctor's.

SOCRATES. And what about when Homer speaks of fishing? "As a leaden weight plunges to the bottom through the horn Of a field-dwelling ox, bringing doom to the ravenous fish." Is it the art of the fisherman or the rhapsode to judge if this is described correctly?
ION. Clearly, Socrates, it is the fisherman's art.

div.head: Section 539
div.p: SOCRATES. Then consider this. What if you were questioning me, and you said: "Since you, Socrates, find passages in Homer that belong to different arts, come now, find for me the passages that belong to the diviner and the diviner's art, to see whether Homer describes them well or not." I would easily find them for you. In the Odyssey, the prophet Theoclymenus says: "Wretched men, what evil is this you suffer? Your heads And your faces and your knees are shrouded in night; Lamentation blazes up, and cheeks are wet with tears. The porch is full of ghosts, and the court is full, Hastening to the underworld beneath the darkness. The sun Has perished from the sky, and an evil mist envelops us." And there are many passages in the Iliad too, such as the battle at the wall: "An omen came to them as they were eager to cross, An eagle flying high on the left, dividing the host, Bearing in its talons a huge, blood-red serpent, Alive and still struggling; nor had it yet forgotten the fight. For twisting backward, it struck its captor on the breast By the neck. In agony, the eagle let it drop To the ground, into the midst of the throng, And shrieking loudly, flew away on the breath of the wind." I would say that these passages and others like them are for the diviner to examine and judge.
ION. And you would speak the truth, Socrates.

SOCRATES. You speak the truth too, Ion. Now you do the same for me. Just as I selected passages belonging to the diviner, the doctor, and the fisherman, you search through the Iliad and the Odyssey and pick out for me, Ion, the passages that belong to the rhapsode and the rhapsode's art—the things it is fitting for a rhapsode to examine and judge above all other men.
ION. I say it is all of them, Socrates.

div.head: Section 540
div.p: SOCRATES. You did not say "all of them" earlier, Ion! Are you so forgetful? It is not fitting for a rhapsode to be forgetful.
ION. What have I forgotten?
SOCRATES. Do you not remember agreeing that the art of the rhapsode is different from the art of the charioteer?
ION. I remember.
SOCRATES. And you agreed that because they are different, they will know different things.
ION. Yes.
SOCRATES. Then by your own argument, the rhapsode's art will not know everything, nor will the rhapsode.
ION. Perhaps with the exception of those specialized things, Socrates.
SOCRATES. By "those specialized things," you mean the subjects of the other arts. But if the rhapsode does not know everything, what is it that he does know?

ION. I think he knows what it is fitting for a man to say, and what it is fitting for a woman to say; what a slave should say, and what a freeman should say; what a subject should say, and what a ruler should say.
SOCRATES. Do you mean what is fitting for the ruler of a ship caught in a storm at sea to say? Will the rhapsode know this better than the pilot?
ION. No, the pilot will know that.
SOCRATES. Or what is fitting for a man ruling a sick person to say? Will the rhapsode know better than the doctor?
ION. No, not that either.
SOCRATES. What about a slave? Do you mean what it is fitting for a slave tending a flock of sheep to say to soothe them? Will the rhapsode know this better than the herdsman?
ION. No.
SOCRATES. Or what is fitting for a spinning-woman to say about preparing wool?
ION. No.
SOCRATES. Then what about what it is fitting for a man to say when he is a general exhorting his troops? Will the rhapsode know that?
ION. Yes! That is the sort of thing the rhapsode will know.
SOCRATES. Wait. Is the art of the rhapsode the same as the art of the general?
ION. At least I would know what a general ought to say.

div.head: Section 541
div.p: SOCRATES. Perhaps that is because you also happen to possess the art of the general, Ion. For instance, if you happened to be both a horseman and a lyre-player, you would know good and bad riding. But if I asked you: "By which art do you know good riding? By your horsemanship, or by your lyre-playing?" What would you say?
ION. By my horsemanship.
SOCRATES. And if you knew good lyre-playing, you would agree you know it by your lyre-playing, not your horsemanship.
ION. Yes.
SOCRATES. Since you know military affairs, do you know them by the art of the general, or by the art of the rhapsode?
ION. It seems to me they are the same thing.
SOCRATES. You say they are the same? That the art of the rhapsode and the art of the general are one single art?
ION. I do.
SOCRATES. So whoever is a good rhapsode also turns out to be a good general?
ION. Absolutely, Socrates.
SOCRATES. Then surely whoever is a good general also turns out to be a good rhapsode?
ION. No, I do not think that is true.
SOCRATES. But you do think that whoever is a good rhapsode is also a good general.
ION. I certainly do.
SOCRATES. And are you not the best rhapsode in Greece?
ION. By far, Socrates.
SOCRATES. Are you also the best general in Greece, Ion?
ION. Know it well, Socrates! And I learned that from Homer's poetry.

SOCRATES. Then by the gods, Ion, if you are both the best general and the best rhapsode among the Greeks, why do you spend your time traveling around reciting poetry instead of commanding an army? Do you think the Greeks have a great need for a rhapsode crowned in gold, but no need at all for a general?

ION. My city, Ephesus, is under the rule of your city, Athens, Socrates, so we have no need of our own general. And as for your city or Sparta, you would not elect me as general because you think you are sufficient unto yourselves.
SOCRATES. My dear Ion, have you not heard of Apollodorus of Cyzicus?
ION. Who is he?

SOCRATES. He is a foreigner whom the Athenians often elect as their general. And there is Phanosthenes of Andros, and Heraclides of Clazomenae, who are also foreigners, but because they have demonstrated their merit, Athens elevates them to military command and honors them. Would not Athens elect Ion of Ephesus as general and honor him, if he seemed worthy? Are not the Ephesians originally Athenians anyway? And Ephesus is not a petty city.

div.head: Section 542
div.p: SOCRATES. But the truth is, Ion, if what you say is correct—that you praise Homer by an art and by knowledge—then you are treating me unjustly. You promised to show me your many fine thoughts about Homer, but you are deceiving me. You will not even tell me what subjects you speak so well on, though I have begged you repeatedly to do so. You act like Proteus, transforming into every shape, twisting and turning, until finally you slip away and appear as a general, just so you can avoid demonstrating how wonderfully you are skilled in Homer! If you truly possess this art, then, as I said, you are treating me unjustly by promising to display it and then deceiving me. But if you do not possess an art, and are instead possessed by a divine dispensation from the Muse—so that you say many beautiful things about the poet without possessing any knowledge, exactly as I said about you—then you are not acting unjustly. Choose, then, how you would like me to think of you: as an unjust man, or as a divine one?
ION. There is a great difference, Socrates. It is far more beautiful to be considered divine.
SOCRATES. Then this more beautiful title we grant to you, Ion: you are a divine praiser of Homer, not an expert by art.
